## Why add another model?

Bins can beat a straight line because the relationship is curved. That does
not establish that categories are the best representation. A useful comparison
includes a continuous model that can bend while keeping the original measurements.

A **natural cubic spline** fits connected smooth curves. Its **knots** are the
locations where those curve pieces join. A knot is not a category boundary;
values on either side remain part of a continuous fitted relationship.
The curve becomes linear outside its outer boundary knots on the model's link
scale. In a logistic model that means the log-odds scale, not the probability scale.
[R spline documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/splines/html/ns.html).

In `binwise`, adding `spline_df = 3` includes this comparator under the name
`spline`. Three degrees of freedom is a modest starting amount of flexibility.
Larger values allow more complex shapes and can overfit. It is not an automatic
choice of the best complexity. The original `continuous` model remains the
linear-term reference. For logistic models its terms are linear in log-odds.

Start a fresh R session, load the package, and run these blocks in order. See
the getting-started guide if you need help running code in RStudio.

```{r load-package}
library(binwise)
data("binwise_smooth", package = "binwise")
```

## 1. Create a curved teaching example

We will reuse the existing exposure values and simulated random noise, but
change the known expected outcome to a smooth U-shaped relationship.
The original dataset remains unchanged.

```{r curved-data}
curved <- binwise_smooth
noise <- curved$outcome - curved$expected_outcome
curved$expected_outcome <- 2 + .008 * (curved$exposure - 50)^2
curved$outcome <- curved$expected_outcome + noise
plot(curved$exposure, curved$outcome, pch = 16, cex = .4, col = "grey65",
     xlab = "Exposure", ylab = "Observed outcome")
```

The outcome tends to be higher near both ends and lower in the middle. The
`expected_outcome` column is available only because this is a simulation.
Do not include that teaching aid as a control when predicting the noisy outcome.

## 2. Fit the straight line, spline, and bins

```{r curved-models}
quartiles <- bin_diagnose(curved, "exposure", bins = 4, warn = FALSE)
curved_fit <- bin_interact(
  curved, outcome = "outcome", variables = "exposure",
  schemes = list(quartiles = quartiles), spline_df = 3
)
plot(curved_fit, xlab = "Exposure", main = "A curve can explain why bins beat a line")
curved_fit$comparison
```

The legend identifies three models. `continuous` fits a straight line here.
`spline` can follow the smooth change. `quartiles` fits flat steps that discard
variation inside each interval. All models use the same observations.

Shading shows 95% pointwise confidence intervals for each fitted mean. It
conditions on the specified model and complexity; it does not account for
choosing the preferred degrees of freedom after viewing results. The bands
are not prediction intervals for individual observations, and their overlap
is not a test of whether two model shapes are equivalent.

Read the plain-language assessment and inspect the spline definition.

```{r curved-assessment}
cat(paste(curved_fit$assessment, collapse = "\n\n"))
curved_fit$spline_details
```

The assessment now includes each binned scheme's fit comparison with the spline.
AIC, BIC, and training error still describe the fitted sample. They do not replace
the held-out comparison below. `spline_details` records interior knots, boundary
knots, degrees of freedom, and the number of training observations.

## 3. Compare held-out predictions directly against the spline

```{r curved-validation}
curved_check <- bin_validate(
  curved, outcome = "outcome", variables = "exposure",
  schemes = list(quartiles = list(
    exposure = list(probs = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1))
  )),
  spline_df = 3, reference = "spline", folds = 5, seed = 12, reps = 199
)
curved_check$scores
plot(curved_check, metric = "RMSE",
     main = "Positive differences mean worse predictions than the spline")
```

The RMSE values are approximately 6.76 for the straight line, 4.50 for quartile
bins, and 3.05 for the spline. Lower is better. The bins improve on the straight
line, but the spline does considerably better than the bins. Here, the useful
feature is curvature, and categorization loses information about it.

`reference = "spline"` changes which model is subtracted when computing score
differences. It does not change the fits, folds, or observations scored.
A negative difference favors a candidate over the spline; a positive one favors
the spline. The intervals are paired bootstrap intervals for loss differences
with predictions and folds fixed. They do not cover all uncertainty from
refitting or model selection. Increase `reps` for a final analysis and check
interval stability.

The spline knots and quantile boundaries are estimated **only from training
observations in each fold**. Held-out values reuse the training definitions.
You can inspect the first fold's stored spline information.

```{r fold-details}
curved_check$fold_details[[1]]$spline
curved_check$diagnostics
```

The spline extends linearly on the link scale beyond its training boundary
knots. That defines an extrapolation rule; it does not prove that extrapolation
is accurate. Check coverage, support, and the intended prediction population.

## 4. Do bins still help when there is a real threshold?

The interaction simulation has an outcome whose expected value jumps at zero.
Within each side of that boundary, changes in `x` do not change the expected
outcome when `z` and the control are held fixed. That known rule supplies a
reason to test two categories.

```{r threshold-validation}
data("binwise_interaction", package = "binwise")
threshold_check <- bin_validate(
  binwise_interaction, outcome = "threshold_outcome",
  variables = c("x", "z"), controls = "control",
  schemes = list(threshold = list(x = list(breaks = c(-Inf, 0, Inf)))),
  spline_df = 3, reference = "spline", folds = 5, seed = 12, reps = 199
)
threshold_check$scores
plot(threshold_check, metric = "RMSE", main = "A real jump can favor threshold categories")
```

Here, RMSE is approximately 1.34 for the linear interaction, 1.28 for the spline,
and 1.20 for the threshold categories. The bins still help against this more
flexible comparator. Their advantage follows from this simulated jump; it is
not a general recommendation to bin all variables at zero.

With two focal variables, `spline_df = 3` applies a spline to **both**. The default
interaction includes all products of those basis terms plus their main effects.
This uses 15 focal-predictor terms, plus an intercept and any controls, compared
with three terms for a linear interaction. With limited observations or joint
support, that can be too complex. Set `interaction = FALSE` for additive
splines when that matches your question. The package records fitting failures
rather than silently reducing complexity. Numeric controls remain linear and
additive in all candidates.

For a binary outcome, use `model = "logit"`. Predictions are probabilities,
and validation reports Brier scores and log loss instead of RMSE and MAE.
Lower remains better. The same spline settings and training-only rules apply.

## 5. Readable boundaries are another candidate, not an automatic decision

R's `pretty()` can suggest round boundaries for a descriptive table or plot.
They are useful when communication matters. You can already use them through
`bin_compare()` without installing another package.

```{r pretty-bins}
round_breaks <- pretty(curved$exposure, n = 4)
round_comparison <- bin_compare(
  curved, "exposure", methods = "quantile",
  custom_breaks = list(round_boundaries = round_breaks)
)
round_breaks
round_comparison$bins[, c("scheme", "bin", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

The requested count is approximate, so inspect the actual boundaries and counts.
In this example, round boundaries give five intervals of width 20. These are
convenient labels, not known scientific thresholds.
[R documentation for `pretty()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/pretty.html).

Do not calculate boundaries from the whole dataset and then describe them as
training-only. In validation, custom `breaks` mean fixed, prespecified boundaries.
A rule that learns `pretty()` or clustering boundaries from data must be fitted
inside each training fold, currently through a `fit_predict` callback. Built-in
recipes currently learn quantiles; they do not learn clustering or pretty breaks.

## How to use this comparison responsibly

Choose a small set of plausible schemes and spline complexities before examining
test performance. Searching many alternatives and reporting the winner on the
same test observations exaggerates performance. Use nested validation or a fresh
test set for that selection process.

A single three-degree-of-freedom spline is not every possible continuous model.
Smooth splines also do not automatically preserve a meaningful zero state or
model a discontinuity. A zero indicator plus continuous positive intensity may
be appropriate for another question. Interpretation and prediction are separate
considerations, and none of these comparisons alone identifies a causal effect.

For repeated observations, supply an appropriate grouping column. For temporal
prediction, note that these folds fit on all other folds, including later ones;
this is not forward-only forecasting. Inspect diagnostics before interpreting
scores calculated on only the rows with predictions available from every model.
